references.text: Ezekiel's prophecy about God as the shepherd who himself seeks out his lost sheep: 'I myself will search for my sheep and look after them' ([ref:Esek 34:11-16|Ezekiel 34:11-16]). This is the Old Testament background for Jesus' parable of the lost sheep.

God's accusation against Israel's shepherds who did not seek out the lost: 'You have not sought out the lost' ([ref:Esek 34:3-6|Ezekiel 34:3-6]). In contrast, Jesus shows that as the good shepherd he actively seeks out the one lost sheep.

'We all went astray like sheep; each of us turned to our own way' ([ref:Jes 53:6|Isaiah 53:6]). The prophecy describes humanity's condition as lost sheep, which forms the background for Jesus' parable.

'I have gone astray like a lost sheep. Seek your servant!' ([ref:Sal 119:176|Psalm 119:176]). The psalmist's prayer that God would seek him out as a lost sheep, which Jesus illustrates that God does in the parable.
Matthew's parallel to the parable of the lost sheep ([ref:Matt 18:12-14|Matthew 18:12-14]), where Jesus tells the same parable in the context of not despising 'one of these little ones'.

Jesus saw the crowds and had compassion on them, 'because they were harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd' ([ref:Matt 9:36|Matthew 9:36]). Jesus' compassion for the lost motivates his search for the one who is lost.

Jesus calls himself 'the good shepherd' who gives his life for the sheep and who has other sheep he must also lead ([ref:Joh 10:11-16|John 10:11-16]). The shepherd motif from the parable in Luke 15 is expanded here with Jesus' self-understanding as the good shepherd.

'You were like sheep going astray, but now you have returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls' ([ref:1 Pet 2:25|1 Peter 2:25]). Peter applies the shepherd-and-sheep motif to believers who have turned back to Christ.
'For the Son of Man came to seek out and save the lost' ([ref:Luk 19:10|Luke 19:10]). Jesus' summary of his mission directly mirrors the action in the parable of the lost sheep.
The following parable of the lost coin ([ref:Luk 15:8-10|Luke 15:8-10]) expresses the same point: God's diligent search for what is lost, and the joy at finding it again.
Jacob refers to God as the shepherd: 'God … who has been my shepherd all my life to this day' ([ref:1 Mos 48:15|Genesis 48:15]). The idea of God as shepherd for his people is deeply rooted in the OT.
'The Lord is my shepherd; I shall not want' ([ref:Sal 23:1-3|Psalm 23:1-3]). The classic psalm about God as the shepherd who leads his sheep to places of rest and paths of righteousness.
